title: Ghost of Yōtei: what each part of the world costs
subtitle: Measured on 2026-10-25 at HOME in Ezo (your PS5 save), 1080p, RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, Ryzen 9 7950X. Emulator: Celegans12's yotei/best of 2026-10-24 plus our porter tools.

summary: Short answer. The world is slow because of how many small orders the game sends to the graphics card, not because of one expensive element. Every frame has about 3,000 draws and 2,500 compute jobs, and the emulator spends roughly 0.1 ms of CPU time on each one. On top of that, its threads keep waiting for each other and for the graphics card.

What cutting does. Switching off one element at a time barely changes the frame rate: the main scene pass gives +30%, instanced objects +17%, everything else stays within about 10%. The time saved in one place is lost waiting at the next meeting point between the emulator's threads.

The 5 fps result. Removing many parts at once reaches 5.6 fps, so the goal is reachable by cutting. But at that point the picture breaks: the parts still needed read results the cut parts should have written. The fastest setup that still looks like the game runs at 3.1 fps (no sun shadows, particles or async effects). Running passes only every second or third frame instead of removing them did not save the picture either.

What this means for a real fix. Deleting parts of the game hits a wall around 3 fps. The way forward is to make every draw and compute job cheaper and to remove the waiting between threads. The last section lists the concrete changes, with the two that are already switches in this build.
why_intro: Measured with a timeline trace of 8 frames, CPU sampling of the two main emulator threads and GPU timing per program.
why: The emulator's main thread waits more than it works. Of its 520 ms per frame, about 300 ms are waiting: 158 ms for the draw committer to catch up before compute jobs, 52 ms because the committer's queue is full, 41 ms for async queues and the GPU, 30 ms for the shared GPU lock. Its own translation work is about 200 ms.

Why it waits for the committer. Almost every compute job (about 2,300 per second) misses the emulator's compute cache, because its inputs move every frame. A missed job is prepared on the main thread, and before that the main thread must wait until the committer has recorded every draw in front of it. An existing switch, APS5_PIPELINE_DISPATCH_MISSES, hands these jobs to the committer instead; it gave +14% on the lean configuration.

The committer waits for the graphics card. It records about 1,900 draws per frame (about 340 ms of work) and blocks about 67 ms per frame on GPU results, for example when a draw needs a texture that a compute job just wrote.

Five single stalls of 40-60 ms each. Interior Volumes (one draw that waits for the GPU), Deferred wetness (one compute job that waits for the committer), Cull CS Lights and Ambient Spec Update (async queue 0x38), Directional Shadow Combine (async queue 0x30). Cutting one of them moves the same wait to the next meeting point, which is why single cuts help so little.

The async queues hold the frame too. With every draw and compute job of the main queue removed, the frame still takes 320 ms (3.1 fps), because the main queue waits for the async queues. With everything removed the game runs at 40 fps.
The graphics card itself spends about 190 ms of program time per frame. Particles take about 48 ms, cloth about 40 ms, and the emulator's own upload copies about 41 ms.

Why a removed wait comes back somewhere else. Tonight's deferred stores cut the committer's direct GPU waits from about 90 ms to about 4 ms per frame, yet the frame only got about 5% faster: a new wait of about 70 ms appeared one step later (Recorder.WaitSerial), and the main thread now spends 132 ms per frame on a full committer queue instead of 52 ms. The emulator checks many resources by reading their memory on the CPU, so whenever the graphics card has just written that memory, some thread has to wait for it. The frame is a chain of such waits between the main thread, the committer and the graphics card.

next_intro: Ordered by how much of the frame each one attacks. None of these removes anything from the picture. Details and code references: yotei-work/porter/research-*.md.
next: 1. Stop draining before compute jobs (already a switch). About 1,100 compute jobs per frame miss the emulator's compute cache and are prepared on the main thread after waiting for the committer: 156 us each, 85 us of it the wait. A cache hit would only save about 15 us; handing the missed job to the committer (APS5_PIPELINE_DISPATCH_MISSES) removes the 85 us. Measured: no change on the full game in three alternating repeats (el12), +14% once much of the frame is cut (el5); the committer becomes the next limit.

2. Stop the committer from waiting for the graphics card (new experimental rule). The committer waits about 67 ms per frame for GPU results, mostly to copy storage images back to memory before a label, before a depth-plane store or when an image is created. Recording those copies behind their writer on the GPU instead keeps the order without the wait. Measured: +5.6% on the full game, picture unchanged, 7 of 7 alternating repeats faster (runs el12 and el14; rule deferstores on). The wait then shows up in the pre-syncs (Recorder::WaitSerial, about 70 ms per frame; called through VulkanDevice::WaitRecorded from PresyncDrawDepth for depth metadata and from presync for colour-compression keys): the committer still reads GPU-written metadata on the CPU before those draws. Expanding the depth metadata on the GPU (DepthSurface.cpp expandHtileOnGpu) is the next step on this path.

3. Remember draws across frames. 70-80% of the world's draws repeat with only a small constant block changing. The porter's engine draw cache (branch porter/main) reuses the prepared draw by engine object; in the world it hits only 3% today because of the vertex-fetch pointer words, which is the first fix to make before porting it here.

4. A second committer, or a preparer for compute jobs. Draws already have a preparer thread that builds part of each draw ahead of the committer; compute jobs do not. Splitting their preparation the same way would let the committer keep up once item 1 hands it all the misses.

5. Descriptor heap. Draws that read memory through address tables cost 371 us each in the committer; a descriptor heap with stable indices (the Tsushima PC model, VK_EXT_descriptor_heap on NVIDIA 610+) replaces most of that work.
6. The game's own settings help little. One shadow cascade and a shorter shadow distance gave 0-9%, within the noise; lower detail levels made an older build slower.

glossary.text: One picture. The game builds every frame from scratch: about 3,000 draws and 2,000 compute jobs each time. Frames per second (fps) is how many it finishes each second.
One stage of building the frame, such as shadows, the main scene, lighting or post effects. The game names its passes with debug markers, and those names are used here.
One order to the graphics card: draw this shape with this material. A tree is a few draws, a field of grass is one draw repeated many times.
An order to the graphics card that calculates instead of drawing: culling, lighting tiles, particles, blur. Its results feed later draws.
What a surface is made of: its textures and shader settings (bark, steel, cloth, snow).
A function inside the game's own code that issues draws, for example DrawItem for single objects or DrawInstanced for repeated ones. Found by reverse engineering the game binary.
The emulator thread that reads the game's GPU orders one by one and translates each into PC graphics work. Queue 0 is the main graphics queue; the others are async compute queues.
A second emulator thread that records the translated draws into Vulkan (the PC graphics interface). When a later order needs the result of earlier draws, the queue worker has to wait for it: a drain.
Time a thread waits for the shared GPU lock while another thread holds it.
For these measurements the emulator drops the orders of one element on purpose. The game does not know; the picture just misses that element.
The sun's shadow map is split into several rings around the camera, from fine near the player to coarse far away. Each ring draws the scene again.

config_sections.title: Making it faster without cutting anything
config_sections.intro: Emulator changes measured on the full game, alternating with the unchanged game in the same run (runs el12 and el14 to el16). Each card compares one repeat with the unchanged game measured just before and after it; the text gives the average over all repeats. The pictures are full frames with nothing removed. The scene is not perfectly steady (one round of el16 was slower for every setup), so differences under about 3% are noise.
cards: New rule from tonight (deferstores on): the committer records storage write-backs behind their writer on the graphics card instead of waiting for the card (about 90 per frame). Average over 10 repeats in three runs: +5% (el12 +7.3%, el14 +4.4%, el15 +4.5%), every repeat faster. Picture unchanged.
HTILE masks for queued compute jobs

Bug fix from tonight (APS5_ITEM_HTILE_MASKS): a depth clear queued for the committer now tells the depth code what it wrote, as the other paths already did. Before, the next depth draw stopped and waited for the whole graphics card about 4 times per second. With the fix: 37 waits per 10 s become 0.4. Alone it changes nothing (-0.7%, noise): without deferred stores each wait is short.

Both together. Deferred stores alone make each HTILE wait long (2.6 s of waiting per 10 s, because more work is queued on the card); the HTILE fix removes most of it (0.1-0.2 s), and the committer's busy time drops by 22%. Average +6.5% over the unchanged game (2.00, 2.00, 2.03 vs 1.89 fps), 3 of 3 repeats faster. Picture unchanged.

Adds the existing switch for mitul72's draw-ahead (#6188, off in our setup because it once stalled at boot; switched on here during gameplay): helper threads capture and compile upcoming draws before the main thread gets to them. In el16, 1.96 fps against 1.86 for the unchanged game (+5.5%, 3 of 3 repeats faster), 1-2% above deferred stores + HTILE alone. Picture unchanged.

Adds APS5_PIPELINE_DISPATCH_MISSES (compute jobs that miss the cache are queued for the committer instead of making the main thread wait). No gain on top (1.89 vs 1.88 fps for deferred stores + HTILE alone): most of the waits it should remove come back as waits for queue space.
